name: CR-Diff-09-misc-4.b
generalfeedback:
To solve this question, you will have to use the chain rule <hint>calc_chain_rule</hint> more than once.

Let \(f({{CT:0}})={{CT:1}}\) and \(g({{CT:0}})={{CT:2}}\). Then, \(f({{CT:0}})=e^{(g({{CT:0}}))}\)

\[\begin{array}{rcl}\displaystyle
 \frac{d}{d{{CT:0}}}[{{CT:1}}] &\displaystyle =&\displaystyle  \frac{df}{dg}\cdot \frac{dg}{dx} \\
   &\displaystyle =&\displaystyle  \frac{d}{dg}(e^{g})\cdot \frac{d}{dx}[{{CT:2}}]
 \end{array}\]

To find \[\frac{d}{dx}[{{CT:2}}]\] you have to define a new function: \(h({{CT:0}})={{CT:3}}\), so that \(g({{CT:0}})=h^{{CT:4}}\). So,

\[\begin{array}{rcl}\displaystyle
 \frac{d}{d{{CT:0}}}[{{CT:2}}] &\displaystyle =&\displaystyle  \frac{dg}{dh}\cdot \frac{dh}{d{{CT:0}}} \\
   &\displaystyle =&\displaystyle  \frac{d}{dh}(h^{{CT:4}})\cdot \frac{d}{d{{CT:0}}}({{CT:3}}) \\
   &\displaystyle =&\displaystyle  {{CT:4}}h^{{CT:5}}\cdot ({{CT:6}}) \\
   &\displaystyle =&\displaystyle  {{CT:7}}
 \end{array}\]

So,

\[\begin{array}{rcl}\displaystyle
 \frac{d}{d{{CT:0}}}[{{CT:1}}] &\displaystyle =&\displaystyle  \frac{d}{dg}(e^{g})\cdot \frac{d}{dx}[{{CT:2}}] \\
   &\displaystyle =&\displaystyle  e^g \cdot {{CT:7}} \\
   &\displaystyle =&\displaystyle  e^{{CT:2}}{{CT:7}} \\
   &\displaystyle =&\displaystyle  {{CT:8}}
 \end{array}\]
